title: Er det tid for guttetur?
subtitle: Is it time for a boys’ trip?
lead: A pandemic-era oracle with seven ways to say no. Eventually, it learned one way to say yes.
storyTitle: A distributed system for saying no.
paragraphs: In March 2021, a small website answered a very specific question: was it time for a boys’ trip? A serverless function picked from seven variations of no. The interface did not offer much room for negotiation.
On 27 October, the list of answers changed to a single “Ja!” There was one small complication: the random selection still expected seven answers. The next commit changed the index to zero.

Two commits, one change of outlook, and a remarkably small API. The site served its purpose. This recreation cycles through the seven historical responses so you can find them all. It is not current travel advice.
connection: Related specimen: another small task that acquired several moving parts.

title: Retrospective.fun
subtitle: Every retro remembers the last one.
lead: Teams have conversations. Then another sprint happens. This one tries to keep the useful bits from disappearing between meetings.
storyTitle: Some things are worth bringing up again.
paragraphs: A retrospective is a chance for a team to pause, talk about what happened, and decide what to do differently. The conversation can be useful. Remembering what came out of it is another matter.

Retrospective.fun is a living application built around that gap: structured conversations, action items, and context carried from one session to the next. Different retrospective formats get their own sequence instead of being squeezed into the same meeting.
Development began in 2017. The experiment is still evolving. The question underneath it remains fairly small: what would change if the next conversation remembered the previous one?
connection: Another kind of continuity: an unfinished idea picked up by another developer.

kind: An idea with a second life
title: NoteGame → NoteQuest
subtitle: Same curiosity. Another pair of hands.
lead: I started a note-reading game. A few years later, my daughter took the idea further. She builds the game. I help with the machinery underneath.
storyTitle: An unfinished idea is not always an ending.
paragraphs: The first experiment was NoteGame: notes on a staff, a choice of answers, a few points for getting them right. It stayed an experiment.
My daughter subsequently took the idea further as NoteQuest, using AI-assisted development. She develops the game; I provide the backend, infrastructure, and heavier engineering support.
It is her implementation of an idea we now share. The original did not need a grand plan for a revival. It needed another developer who wanted to make something of it.
connection: A shared thread: carrying something useful into what comes next.
